title: Make Matrix use DomainMatrix internally
description:

#### Brief description of what is fixed or changed

This is a work in progress PR to change the internal representation of `Matrix` from the current `._mat` list of `Expr` to a `._rep` DomainMatrix attribute. The `DomainMatrix` still uses `Expr` internally via the `EXRAW` domain added in #21581.

#### Other comments

I am using this PR as a staging area and spinning out most changes to sub-PRs like #21632, #21633, #21637 to keep the diff small for the main change.

The internal `DomainMatrix` can use either the `ZZ`, `QQ` or `EXRAW` domains for elementary arithmetic like matrix multiplication. The `DomainMatrix` sparse implementation is used and can make other operations like `zeros`, `eye` etc more efficient.

Using domains like `ZZ[x,y]` for elementary operations is not backwards compatible because e.g. these domains will automatically expand any powers. However if the internal representation is a sparse DomainMatrix with domain EXRAW then we can efficiently convert to something like `ZZ[x,y]` where it is beneficial as part of an algorithm such as `charpoly`.

I have unified most of the implementation of DenseMatrix and SparseMatrix into a class RepMatrix with an inheritance scheme like:

```python
class RepMatrix(MatrixBase):
    # methods using DomainMatrix
    # Most implementation of matrix classes is here

class MutableRepMatrix(RepMatrix):
    # mutation methods

class ImmutableRepMatrix(RepMatrix, MatrixExpr):
    # a few specialisations for immutable

class DenseMatrix(RepMatrix):
   # Methods specific to dense

class SparseMatrix(RepMatrix):
    # methods specific to sparse
    
class MutableDenseMatrix(DenseMatrix, MutableRepMatrix):
    # 1 method (simplify) specific to this class

class MutableSparseMatrix(SparseMatrix, MutableRepMatrix):
    # 1 method (_new) specific to this case

class ImmutableDenseMatrix(DenseMatrix, ImmutableRepMatrix):
    # A few methods for immutable dense

class ImmutableSparseMatrix(SparseMatrix, ImmutableRepMatrix):
    # A few methods for immutable sparse
```
Internally all of these classes use DomainMatrix with its internal sparse representation (SDM) so there isn't much benefit in having SparseMatrix and DenseMatrix as separate classes. I've mostly unified the implementation of matrices into RepMatrix. Sparse and dense mutable matrices are reasonably unified in MutableRepMatrix. There are only small differences between ImmutableDenseMatrix and ImmutableSparseMatrix but since those differences concern the constructor arguments they are not immediately easy to resolve. Further unification of these classes is deferred for now.


TODO:

- [x] Detect ZZ, QQ domains instead of always using EXRAW.
- [x] Make use of DomainMatrix methods for speed.
- [x] Convert SparseMatrix to use DomainMatrix as well
- [x] Move most methods from DenseMatrix/SparseMatrix up to MatrixBase
- [ ] ~~Make the args of ImmutableDenseMatrix sparse~~
- [ ] ~~Convert ImmutableSparseMatrix args to the same form as for dense~~
- [x] Unify Mutable-dense/sparse.
- [ ] ~~Unify Immutable-dense/sparse~~
- [x] Identify methods that are inconsistent between dense/sparse
- [x] Run benchmarks
- [x] Re-add `_mat` and `_smat` with deprecation warnings

#### Release Notes

and the release note for this PR. For example:

* functions

or if no release note(s) should be included use:

NO ENTRY

See https://github.com/sympy/sympy/wiki/Writing-Release-Notes for more
information on how to write release notes. The bot will check your release

<!-- BEGIN RELEASE NOTES -->
* matrices
    * The internal implementation of Matrix and other matrix classes (SparseMatrix etc) is now DomainMatrix. The ZZ and QQ domains are used for matrices with only integer or rational elements. Otherwise the new EXRAW domain is used. This should be backwards compatible although many internal methods and attributes are changed. At the time of this change the DomainMatrix routines are only used for addition and multiplication of matrices and some other simple low-level operations. Further changes will use DomainMatrix routines for operations like `rref`, `det`, `lu` etc and are expected to lead to big speedups for these computations. At this stage those big speedups are not realised but some basic operations such as indexing a matrix like `M[0, 0]` could potentially be slower. The new implementation can be much faster for most operations and is expected to lead to significant speed ups over the next few SymPy releases.

A benchmark comparison against current master is below. The results are mixed but that is expected. The change here means that the Matrix class is internally more efficient but routines that operate on the matrix manually from outside are slower. For example getitem is slower and many routines that use getitem are slower as a result but the eventual plan would be to replace those routines with lower-level routines that operate directly on the more efficient internal representation.

The timings below would suggest that det is slower with this PR but actually this can make det much faster. However the new routines can be a little slower for some very small e.g. 1x1 matrices. The current benchmark suite mainly tests trivially tiny examples that are unlikely to be relevant to the performance of any real work usage so it might seem to show slowdowns for this PR.

This PR does not yet employ the low-level routines for any significant operations like `det`, `inv`,  etc but it represents the first step towards a more efficient implementation. It is expected that there will be small slowdowns here and that speedups from these changes will not yet show in the benchmarks. I want to merge this though and then work on operations like `det` one by one.

comments.body:
I was intending to squash the commits but I now think that they should not be squashed or rearranged. This PR makes major changes to matrices but the commits are organised as incremental changes with each step representing a mostly working state of the code. Preserving these commits would be useful for bisecting bugs or regressions.

This PR represents the first step in a major improvement in the performance of the main matrix subclasses by basing them on the more efficient DomainMatrix class. In this PR the change is that the internal representation of Matrix etc is made to be DomainMatrix. That change will speed up some elementary operations but will also slow down some others. Future changes building on this can speed up many common routines but those are not implemented in this PR.

The most noticeable performance improvement with this PR is for sparse matrices. This PR makes Matrix use DomainMatrix internally and specifically uses the SDM sparse internal representation of DomainMatrix. That means that basic matrix arithmetic is made more efficient for sparse matrices.

Example with the PR:
```python
In [1]: M = randMatrix(100, percent=1)

In [2]: %time ok = M*M
CPU times: user 458 µs, sys: 29 µs, total: 487 µs
Wall time: 496 µs
```
Timings with master:
```python
In [2]: %time ok = M*M
CPU times: user 1.75 s, sys: 16 ms, total: 1.77 s
Wall time: 1.78 s
```
That's a speed difference of more than 1000x.

The other performance improvement is for matrices of integer/rational.

Example with the PR:
```python
In [1]: M = randMatrix(100)

In [2]: %time ok = M*M
CPU times: user 289 ms, sys: 2.25 ms, total: 291 ms
Wall time: 290 ms
```
Timing for master:
```python
In [5]: M = randMatrix(100)

In [6]: %time ok = M*M
CPU times: user 12.9 s, sys: 284 ms, total: 13.1 s
Wall time: 13.5 s
```
That's a 50x speed difference for this case.

This is just the start of a process. The new implementation is much faster but we have to switch various functions to use it internally. Right now this PR changes it so that the Matrix class uses DomainMatrix as its internal representation but does not use the DomainMatrix routines for anything except basic things like addition and multiplication. This is already quite a big diff though so I don't want to change all of the other things at the same time. Also some of the changes would potentially lead to different output being returned and in this PR I am trying not to change any behaviour of Matrix.

The goal here is to switch the internal implementation while making as few other changes as possible and hopefully without causing any major slowdown although there can be small slowdowns for some relatively trivial operation.

> For example with LUSolve you have an O(n^3) relationship based on size of the matrix. I'm -1 on adding that kind of major slowdown.

The benchmarks are unfortunately not always representative. I am interested in some kind of genuine slowdown and the benchmarks can help identify those but those particular changes are not indicative of what this change really means for LUsolve performance in sympy.

So you see that the actual time to compute the LU decomposition (the first call to LUsolve) takes basically the same amount of time. When the result is cached then some small difference in the time to index a matrix or something comes into it. I can probably optimise that just to make the benchmark look better but this is not how we will actually speed up the LU decomposition.

The internal DomainMatrix class has its own `lu_solve` function but we are not using that here yet:
```python
In [7]: %time ok = M._rep.lu_solve(b._rep)
CPU times: user 796 µs, sys: 0 ns, total: 796 µs
```

That's how long it takes after caching so you can see that it is faster than what is currently timed by the benchmarks. That is not what is really supposed to speed things up with DomainMatrix though which is when we use a specific domain. That's how we can get it to be faster for the first call to LUsolve which is the one that we care about:

> The main case I'm worried about are operations on dense matrices with symbolic expressions as the elements. The `randMatrix()` function you show creates numerical matrices, so I don't know if those examples represent symbolic matrices also.

The slowdown that you are seeing in the benchmarks is essentially that there is a little extra overhead in setting items in the matrix. I think particularly the LUsolve function uses a lot of slice assignment like `M[i,j:N] = some_list` or something like that which is not a case that I tried to optimise here. That could be made faster but if that is a dominant factor in the routine then it suggests that the routine can be made faster still if it just uses lists directly rather than matrix assignment. It shows up as being significant only after caching because otherwise if your matrices have significant symbolic expressions then the cost of slice assignment will be dwarfed by the other calculations.

Where something like the cost of that slice assignment is likely to be noticeable is if your matrix has simple elements like integers which is why I demonstrate that DomainMatrix is already much faster in that case.

Your PyDy examples are matrices with many symbols and also sin/cos terms. The sin/cos are not something that DomainMatrix can handle properly with a domain yet (https://github.com/sympy/sympy/issues/20608) so until that is resolved the EX or EXRAW domains would need to be used which negates the main benefit of DomainMatrix. The old routines can continue to be used though so I don't expect that you will see any significant difference in those cases (unless a significant regression is overlooked somewhere).

The reason this PR does not immediately make use of all the DomainMatrix routines is that each one needs to be considered carefully for what kinds of expressions it should be used with and what domains should be used and how the user can select between the different routines and so on.

I've tried looking into the other slowdowns indicated by the benchmarks but:

1. The particular benchmark results are not really representative of actual performance due to cacheing.
2. The slowdowns are seen in benchmarks with very small matrices and are not replicated for larger matrices. From my testing so far any potential change that improves one of the benchmarks slows down handling larger matrices.
3. Cases like det/rank can be much faster if the DomainMatrix routines are used but I don't want to enable that in this PR.

I think at this stage we should just accept these "slowdowns" (as suggested by the benchmarks) and merge this so that further work optimising matrix performance can continue.

Maybe also the cache should be disabled for the benchmark timings because they are very much not representative of the actual time to perform a particular calculation *once* which is actually what matters.

review_comments.body: Is this better than making it an attribute that is set to `tuple(self)`? If I understand correctly, every call to `_flat` will return a unique, mutable copy of self's elements.

review_comments.author: oscarbenjamin
review_comments.body:
Yes, returning a tuple might be better.

What isn't clear to me is how much we need to respect backwards compatibility wrt `_mat` which is technically private but is also used widely in the SymPy codebase and potentially other downstream code as well. It isn't possible to maintain full backwards compatibility because `_mat` can be modified directly as a way of mutating the Matrix. If we take out the possibility that someone is using `_mat` to mutate the Matrix then returning a list is best for backwards compatibility.

But what if someone is mutating the list? Should we raise a warning or make sure that the operation completely fails (which would be the case if a tuple was returned)?

review_comments.author: oscarbenjamin
review_comments.body:
Actually for mutable matrices we need to construct the list/tuple each time. In the case of immutable matrices a tuple could be stored. Perhaps it could be a tuple in all cases even though it would have to be created fresh each time for mutable matrices.

The performance here should not matter much in the end since the intention is that DomainMatrix would end up handling each of the operations that currently accesses `._mat`.
